explain.say: Imagine walking down a street in Chennai at sunrise. On almost every doorstep is a beautiful white pattern, freshly drawn that morning. It is called a kolam, and in many parts of India, coloured versions are called rangoli. Look at the board: let us make one together.

explain.say: Beautiful work! Wow fact: kolams are made of rice flour so ants and birds can eat them, a little gift for small creatures, and during the Pongal harvest festival some fill whole streets. Mathematicians even study kolams to learn about patterns. Challenge: make a kolam with a 3 by 3 grid of dots.

faq.a: Rangoli is a decorative floor pattern made in India and Nepal with coloured powders, rice, sand or flower petals, especially for festivals like Diwali, to welcome guests and good fortune.
asks: Why do people make rangoli at Diwali?

faq.q: How do you draw a kolam?
faq.a: Clean the floor, place a grid of rice flour dots, then draw curving lines that loop around the dots, often as one continuous line that returns to where it began.
asks: How to make a dot pattern rangoli

faq.q: What is the difference between rangoli and kolam?
faq.a: Kolam is the South Indian tradition, especially in Tamil Nadu, of white rice flour line patterns around dots, often made daily. Rangoli is the wider name for colourful floor art made across India for festivals.
asks: Is kolam the same as rangoli?

faq.q: Why are kolams drawn with rice flour?
faq.a: Rice flour is easy to pour in fine lines, and it also feeds ants, birds and other small creatures, which is seen as a kind act to start the day.

faq.q: What does symmetry mean in rangoli?
faq.a: Symmetry means one part matches another, like a mirror image or a pattern that looks the same when turned. Most rangoli and kolam designs have strong symmetry.

facts: Kolam patterns in Tamil Nadu are traditionally drawn with rice flour on the threshold of homes.
Rangoli is widely made for Diwali, the festival of lights.
